# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original landscape in the manner of Caspar David
Friedrich, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. The place,
subject and composition are yours to invent. Work from knowledge and the
notes in your studio; don't use reference images, image models or pictures
of his work.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- You paint at the easel: paint a chunk, look at the canvas, paint the
  next. Its tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- What is painted stays painted. There is no undo: paint over what you
  don't want.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count. The
  clock isn't a budget or a target.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by reflecting,
  flipping, rotating or translating another mask's or stroke's coordinates.
  A shape that mirrors another is drawn as its own shape, not as
  `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or `m:at(W - x, y)`.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced);
notes/research/trees.md (how trees are built) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  Entries stay as written.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

- day 1, 09:00: Plan (before any paint). Subject: a lagoon at dusk, seen from a raised bank. Low horizon (~2/3 down), huge graded sky (smalt zenith -> green-grey -> apricot glow where the sun has just gone), still water carrying the glow, a far shore with a ruined gable and three dark firs (hope against ruin), and on the left a stag-headed old oak, black against the light, the tallest thing in the picture. One small figure seen from behind at the water's edge, birds, an evening star last. Method after Friedrich: warm two-layer ground (red/ochre knife layer, whitish brushed top layer), light graphite underdrawing, very thin underpainting, thin layers with stippled gradations, tree twigs and figure last with a pointed brush. First: test swatches in the bottom strip that the dark foreground will cover later, to learn what the piles do.
- day 1, 11:03: Findings so far. (1) Ground: cream, warm; thin blues over it come out light and slightly greyed (smalt 3 : cobalt 1 : white 1.2 reads as a mid periwinkle-blue, not dark). (2) Sky lay-in: horizontal bands with hand=broad, coverage 3, fill=true, then one blend(angle=0) pass over the whole area gives a smooth gradation in one go; bands alone look like separate stripes. (3) blend() is not clipped to what I mean: it dragged my swatches at the bottom because they were still wet; the mask I gave covered them. (4) Cloud bars painted with a flat brush from a single load are thin and hard; hand-drawn outline + work(body) + blend gives a soft bank, but heavy grey; keep those banks thin. (5) Underdrawing in H pencil is nearly invisible at whole-canvas view, fine as a guide. Sky is now bands of smalt -> pale blue -> lime -> pale yellow -> apricot; water below the horizon is a rough echo of it. All still wet; will let it dry a day before glazing.
- day 3, 09:47: Mistake: blended a glow glaze with a mask that included the far shore I had painted ten minutes earlier; the blender dragged the still-open shore into a grey smear right of x=500. Blend masks must exclude fresh wet paint, and each layer should be left to dry before the next goes near it. Will let it dry and repaint the far shore (crowns, ruin, firs) with clipped passes and no big blends. The smear does make a nice mist bank near the sun, so I will keep some of that as haze.
- day 10, 00:44: Second time the blender bit me: I blended the water glaze with a mask that excluded the bank (rect - BANK), but the badger still dragged the wet bank edge out onto the water (dark haze) and pale streaks into the bank. Rule for the rest of the picture: never run blend() within ~25 units of anything wet; use glaze/stipple with clip masks near edges and let each passage dry first. Plan: wait 3 days, then repaint the bank edge opaque with a clipped mask (pushed a few units outward if needed to cover the haze), then water ripples, then the oak on a dry bank.
- day 15, 02:05: Day 15 assessment. Too pale and chalky in the middle band: my lead-white glazes (veil, mist) made a flat cream slab where the far shore should be dark and crisp; the SH3 band I added on top is a lilac stripe with a hard lower edge. Blue->yellow seam in the sky is still too abrupt, and the two cloud bars have round pill ends. Plan: (1) wait for dry, (2) repaint the far land as one opaque band with a hand-drawn tree line, crisp waterline, ruin and firs standing in it, mist as a thin stippled veil at its foot; (3) transparent warm glazes (chrome yellow + vermilion, lots of medium) for luminous glow instead of white veils; teal glaze between blue and yellow; (4) reflections in the water: dark shore reflection, column of glow, horizontal ripples, cloud reflections drawn fresh; (5) only then the oak, bank texture, figure.
- day 29, 17:16: Day 29 sky rework: laid the upper sky again in five bands (smalt/cobalt/Prussian to pale blue to lemon) and one blend pass; it is now a smooth gradation from deep blue to a lemon and gold glow, which is what I wanted. Warm glazes of gold/orange (lots of medium) over the horizon zone worked far better than the white veils. Side effect: the glazes went over the ruin and firs (they stand above the shore band mask) and washed them out; they must be repainted once dry. Next: wait; ruin and firs again; a few thin cloud strata; then the water (glow column, ripples), the bank, the oak, the figure.
- day 47, 07:44: Day 47. The oak works. Recipe that finally gave a convincing bare oak: (1) main limbs hand-placed as Catmull-Rom control points with widths, turned into polygons with a bark-noise wobble and filled with work(hand=detail, clip=true) in two passes; (2) twigs by a zigzag sympodial generator: each axis turns alternately left and right at every elbow, a side shoot leaves on the outside of each elbow, child width 0.5-0.78 of the local parent width, upward tropism small, sparser in the dead top; 668 twigs; (3) twigs wider than 1.8 units are filled as clipped polygons (a round brush along a curved path splits into bristle fans and looks like hair), thinner ones are single rigger strokes with pressure falling to 0 so they end in a point. Also: functions defined with `local` in one chunk do not exist in the next (widthAt, angfn) - define helpers as globals. To do: trunk modelling with rim light from the glow, bank texture and reeds, the figure, glow column and ripples in the water, thin cloud strata, darker ruin, birds, evening star.
- day 47, 09:29: Day 47 review, before the last stage. Working: oak, sky gradient, low horizon, mood. Weak: (1) water is a flat pale slab as bright as the sky and lightest at lower right, where it should be darkest and coolest (it reflects the upper sky); needs a glow column under the sun, ripple streaks, dark edge under the bank; (2) ruin and firs are pale lilac ghosts, need a bit more value so the focal point reads; a luminous gap between two cloud strata above the ruin would concentrate the light; (3) bank is a featureless dark shape: needs reeds, tufts, crest light; (4) trunk needs bark fissures and warm edge light; (5) no figure yet: about 48 units tall at the crest x=352, y=607.5 (scale checked: trunk 1.5 m = 60 units at y=650 gives 40 units/m; eye 4 m above the water); (6) birds and an evening star last. Everything I just painted is wet: wait a week before glazing near the bank or tree.
- day 59, 10:38: Day 59 status. Water: the cool glaze gave the lower water a proper blue, but the badger left it blotchy with weave dots; acceptable as ripple texture, will add fine horizontal ripple marks. Far shore: a misty glaze softened everything and the ruin now reads as a faint ghost; want the ruin and firs a little darker again (detail brush, dry). Composition thoughts: the oak is the mass on the left; the right is open sky and water, so what carries the eye is the line of the water to the ruin. Add: a row of fishing stakes receding from the bank toward the ruin (perspective: heights ~30, 22, 16, 11, 8, 6) and one figure at the crest beside the oak. No boat: too many things. Sky: a thin lilac cloud strip above the ruin, a few high cirrus streaks, birds, and the evening star last. Wait a week for the glazes and the trunk repaint to dry first.
- day 68, 11:11: Mistake on day 68: repainting the horizon zone opaque with mask rect - TREEM covered the fine twigs that reach down to y=405-490 on the left (only the big limbs were in TREEM) and, as planned but sooner than it should have been, the whole far shore. Twigs are not lost: BR2 / BR still hold their coordinates, so after the new ground has dried I can repaint every twig that reaches below y=400 with paint_twig. Then repaint the far shore darker (the glaze veil earlier washed it into a ghost: use value, and put haze only at the foot), redo ruin/firs with a dark value against the glow, add radial glow core over the sky only, then water ripples, stakes, reeds, figure, birds, star. Lesson: any mask that says 'not the tree' must include the twigs; build TWALL from all twig ribbons once and keep it.
- day 81, 19:31: Day 81 disaster, again the same cause: I laid the glow-column glaze over the water ten minutes after working the wet bank crest and painting the reeds. The glaze brush lifted the wet dark and dragged it across the water in long smears, and smeared the reeds into black fans. The lower half of the water is spoiled. Repair plan: wait until everything is bone dry, then repaint the water as opaque body-colour bands (clip to water only, blend only where I am >8 units from the bank), re-lay the far-shore reflection, glow column, ripples; then repaint the bank edge and redo grass and reeds on dry paint. From now on: after touching the bank, tree or reeds, do NOT run any glaze/blend near them until dry. Always check drying() at the edge first.
- day 95, 23:31: Day 95 check (value, squint). Structure is right: dark oak left, pale glow right, ruin as a small pale accent. Problems: (a) the glow zone and water are one flat pale slab: no cloud strata, no darker water toward the viewer, so the light does not glow; (b) grass tufts and reeds on the bank were covered when I re-laid the water (they stand in the water's mask); redo them on dry paint; (c) far-shore reflection lost; (d) trunk is a flat black shape: needs warm edge light on the sun side; (e) figure, birds, star still to come. Waiting a week so twigs, hairs and water are dry before going near them.
- day 104, 03:48: Day 104 mishap: repainting the sky between the blue and the lemon over x=200-1010, I used a mask (SKB) that did not exclude the tree, so opaque sky went over the upper crown and the blend smeared the wet sky into a dark cloud where the tree had been. I have the coordinates of every limb (OAK2_MASKS), twig (BR, BR2) and hair (HAIR_OLD, HAIR), so nothing is lost: plan is (1) wait for it to dry, (2) repaint the whole sky from y=55 to y=345 across the full width with the same five piles in bands and one blend (no seams), (3) wait, (4) re-ink every limb, twig and hair that reaches above y=350, (5) only then clouds, birds, star. Also: the tree repaint order is thick limbs (masks, round 3, OK.deep), twigs by paint_twig, hairs by paint_hair. Never again run work() on a full-width sky rectangle without subtracting the tree unless I mean to re-ink it.
- day 129, 16:58: Day 129: repeated the same class of mistake, this time by omission. The water glazes (cool deepening + glow column) were masked with rect - BANK2 - TREEALL, but the figure, the grass blades and reeds stand on water pixels above the crest, so the glaze veiled them grey; and the column glaze, unblended, left blotchy pale pools (loaded stroke starts). Decision: let it dry, re-lay the water in opaque bands with darker/cooler lower bands and a warm column as its own pass, blend once, then re-ink hanging twigs, re-run the grass and figure chunks exactly (same seeds, so identical marks), and only then add ripples and the far-shore reflection with small dry strokes. Lesson to keep: any object standing in front of the water needs to be in the exclusion mask, or be painted after the water.
- day 135, 17:52: Day 135. Re-laid the water wet-in-wet in six bands + a column; the blend averaged the lower blue bands into the pale ones, so the lower water is pale again, and the figure/grass/hanging twigs are veiled (they stand on water pixels). Not touching anything near it until dry. # The easel

The easel is a live oil painting. You send it Lua chunks with its `paint`
tool, one at a time, and look at the canvas between them with `look`. Under it is a physical paint simulator: simulated
bristles carry wet paint over a primed linen canvas, the paint levels and
dries on a clock, and layers combine by Kubelka–Munk optics.

Three things hold for every session:

- **Every chunk that runs stays on the canvas.** There is no undo. To
  change something, paint over it.
- **A chunk that stops with an error changes nothing.** The canvas, your
  variables, the paint on your brushes and the clock are as they were
  before it, and it isn't written to the log.
- **The log is the painting.** Every chunk that ran is appended to
  `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, and replaying it paints the same canvas.

## Starting

The studio holds one painting, and the easel is open on it. Its tools:

| tool | what it does |
|---|---|
| `paint` | runs a chunk of Lua. The reply is what the chunk printed, then `ok · chunk N` |
| `look` | shows you the canvas as it is now (see [Looking](#looking)) |
| `note` | adds an entry to your journal (see [The journal](#the-journal)) |
| `status` | the number of chunks, the canvas width in pixels and the canvas's setup |
| `log` | the painting so far: every chunk that ran, each after a line `--@ chunk N` |

The first chunk is `canvas{}` (see [The canvas](#the-canvas)). The canvas
is 2400 pixels wide. `read` reads the files in this folder: your brief and
your notes.

In the examples below, `<tube>` stands for a name from the tube box and
`<parts>` for a number of parts you choose.

## The canvas

```lua
canvas{size=<mm>, aspect=<width / height>, linen={16, 14}, seed=1,
       ground={{pile={{"<tube>", <parts>}, {"<tube>", <parts>}}, um=100, apply="knife", texture=0.3},
               {pile={{"<tube>", <parts>}}, um=50, apply="brush"}}}
```

- `size`: the canvas's width in mm (50 to 5000).
- `aspect`: width / height.
- `linen`: plain-weave linen, threads per cm, one number or `{warp, weft}`
  (4 to 60).
- `ground`: the preparation layers, bottom first. Each is a paste mixed
  from tubes in parts (as a pile is, below), a thickness in µm (5 to 400)
  and how it is put on: `"knife"` (levels the weave; `texture` 0..1 is the
  knife's waviness), `"roller"` (a fine even texture) or `"brush"` (laid in
  crossing strokes, its striations stay). The ground is dry when painting
  starts.
- `seed`: the randomness of the linen, the ground and everything after.

It sets `W` (1000) and `H` (`1000 / aspect`). The canvas is always 1000
units wide, whatever its pixel width. The origin `(0, 0)` is the upper
left corner; x increases to the right and y downward. Angles are radians,
0 left to right, π/2 downward.

## Tubes and piles

Paint reaches the canvas only from piles you knife together on the
palette from the tubes in the box:

```lua
p = pile{{"<tube>", <parts>}, {"<tube>", <parts>}}
q = pile{{"<tube>", <parts>}, medium=0.3}
print(p)                         -- pile(<tube> <parts>, <tube> <parts>; medium 0)
print(table.concat(tubes(), ", "))   -- the names in the box
```

A pile is parts by volume of named tubes, plus `medium`: the share of oil
medium mixed in (0, as from the tube, to 0.95). Medium makes the paint more
transparent and more fluid, and slower to dry. What a pile looks like is
what its pigments make together, thick or thin, over what is already on
the canvas; you find out by painting with it and looking. A pile mixed by
hand is a little uneven: each brushload takes slightly different
proportions (about 6%). The palette has room for 16 piles; the oldest is
scraped off to make room.

The tube box:

| tube | pigment | hiding | stiffness | tinting strength | drying |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lead white | basic lead carbonate | 0.82 | 0.8 | 1.0 | 2.0 |
| smalt | cobalt potash glass, coarse | 0.3 | 0.55 | 0.45 | 1.6 |
| pale smalt | a paler grade of smalt | 0.35 | 0.55 | 0.35 | 1.6 |
| yellow ochre | hydrated iron oxide earth | 0.8 | 0.7 | 0.8 | 0.8 |
| red earth | iron oxide earth | 0.85 | 0.7 | 0.9 | 1.0 |
| vermilion | mercuric sulfide | 0.9 | 0.75 | 1.0 | 0.4 |
| raw umber | iron and manganese oxide earth | 0.8 | 0.65 | 0.9 | 2.4 |
| bone black | charred bone (carbon, calcium phosphate) | 0.9 | 0.7 | 1.1 | 0.4 |
| cobalt blue | cobalt aluminate | 0.55 | 0.6 | 0.8 | 1.4 |
| chrome yellow | lead chromate | 0.9 | 0.7 | 1.0 | 1.8 |
| Prussian blue | iron ferrocyanide | 0.35 | 0.45 | 3.0 | 1.8 |
| green earth | celadonite and glauconite clay | 0.2 | 0.35 | 0.3 | 0.8 |
| Rinmann's green | cobalt-zinc oxide | 0.35 | 0.5 | 0.4 | 1.4 |
| copper green | verdigris ground in oil | 0.25 | 0.4 | 1.0 | 1.6 |

Hiding is how much one coat of the tube paint hides what is under it (0
transparent, 1 opaque). Stiffness is the paint's body as it comes from the
tube (0 fluid, 1 stiff). Tinting strength is relative to an average
pigment. Drying is the rate relative to average paint (higher dries
faster); a pile dries at its tubes' rates mixed by volume. These numbers
are estimates from the pigment literature, not measurements.

## Brushes and strokes

```lua
b = brush("filbert", 8)                  -- kinds: round, flat, filbert, fan, rigger, badger, stippler
b = brush{kind="round", width=3, point=1, stiffness=0.5}   -- also length, hair, run, lay, pickup,
                                                           -- push, splay, ragged, bristles
b:load(p, 0.8)                           -- dip into a pile: 0..1 of a full load
b:reload(q, 0.8)                         -- wipe most of the old paint off, then load
b:wipe(0.85)                             -- remove 85% of the paint onto the rag
b:fullness()                             -- paint left, 0..1
b:stroke({{120, 640}, {260, 470}, {430, 420}},
  {pressure={0.9, 0.3}, ramps={0.05, 0.4}, orient="across", shake=1, swell={1, 1.3, 0.8}, clip=m})
b:touch(400, 300, {pressure=0.6, drag={1, 0}, twist=0.2, angle=0.3, clip=m})
b:mark_width(0.4)                        -- the width of a mark at this pressure (units)
b:pressure_for(0.5)                      -- the pressure for a 0.5-unit line
```

Widths are in canvas units. A brush keeps its paint across strokes and
chunks, so strokes from one load run dry, and a brush that has been
through wet paint carries some of it. Pressure ranges from 0 (lifted)
to 1 (fully pressed); a stroke's `pressure` is `{start, end}`.
`ramps` gives the press-down and lift-off fractions, `swell` pressure factors
along the stroke, `orient` `"across"`, `"along"` or a fixed angle.

Brushes are blunt unless given a `point` (0 blunt, 1 a full point). A
pointed round or rigger lays a hairline at light pressure and spreads to
its belly when pressed, so its width follows the pressure and a stroke
whose pressure falls to 0 ends in a point.

## Covering an area

```lua
work(m, {hand="body", pile=p, angle=0.3, coverage=3})
blend(m, {angle=0})                      -- a clean blender over wet paint (= work with hand="blend")
stipple(m, {pile=p, width=3, coverage=1.2})
work(m, {hand="glaze", pile=q})          -- a thin layer brushed on with a soft brush
lose(m, {pile=p, where=0.5})
```

`work` covers a mask with strokes of a real brush, planned the way a hand
lays them. `hand` picks a starting handling, which the options below
change:

| hand | tool | strokes |
|---|---|---|
| `broad` | filbert 22 | 80–220 units, bowing in long arcs, direction wandering over 350-unit patches |
| `body` (default) | filbert 9 | 20–60 units |
| `detail` | round 2.2 | 4–14 units, clipped to the mask |
| `hatch` | round 2.6 | 5–12 units, nearly straight, side by side, clumped |
| `glaze` | soft filbert 26 | 120–300 units, light pressure |
| `scumble` | filbert 9 | 10–20 units, worked back and forth |
| `blend` | badger 40 | a clean blender, crossing passes top to bottom, inside the mask |

| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `pile` | the pile every stroke dips into (every hand but `blend`) |
| `tool` | `"filbert 8"`, `{kind=, width=, ...}` or a brush |
| `length` | `{min, max}` stroke length in units |
| `coverage` | layers of strokes over each point on average |
| `angle` | stroke direction: a number or `function(x, y)` |
| `pressure`, `ramps` | `{min, max}` pressure; attack and release fractions |
| `dips` | `{strokes per trip to the palette, load, wipe before dipping}` |
| `load`, `load_at` | load per dip; a number or `function(x, y)` that varies it |
| `edge` | how the passage meets the mask's edge (below) |
| `clip` | `true`: every bristle stops on the mask's edge; or a mask to clip to |
| `hug` | `true` (default): strokes reach the mask's edges; `false` lets coverage thin there |
| `fill` | `false` by default: gaps between strokes stay. Set `true` to follow the strokes with dabs into the gaps they left |
| `order` | `"passages"` (default), `"scatter"`, `"down"`, `"across"` or a sweep angle |
| `angle_jitter`, `curve` (`{bow, wave}`), `cross`, `drift` (`{amount, scale}`), `tail`, `broken`, `swell`, `clump`, `ruler` | how far the strokes depart from even ruler lines (`ruler=true` sets them straight and even) |
| `orient`, `shake`, `threshold`, `cut_in` (a tool), `scrub`, `blender`, `mix_jitter`, `seed` | the brush's orientation, the hand's unsteadiness, the mask level strokes start at, cutting in the edge with a second tool, back-and-forth strokes, a clean brush, how uneven each dip of the pile is, the randomness |

Where an option takes `function(x, y)`, it is sampled every 2 units over
the area and interpolated. A mistyped option is an error that lists the
valid ones.

**Edges.** `edge=` carries the passage up to the mask's edge the way a
brush does: each stroke stops by its own amount, and past the line its
film thins out over the weave. It takes a number from 0 (found: crisp) to
1 (lost: the passage runs well past the line and dissolves), a name
(`"found"`, `"firm"`, `"soft"`, `"loose"`, `"lost"`), a function of
`(x, y)`, a mask, or a table: `{found=, soft=, lost=, period=40, seed=}`
lays those shares out along the contour in runs about `period` units long;
`waver=` and `reach=` scale how far the line wanders and how far strokes
run over. It can't be combined with `cut_in`.

**`stipple(m, {...})`** lays many small touches of a tip, each through the
bristles: `pile`, `width` (a stippler's width, 2 by default) or `tool`,
`coverage` (touches per point; a number or `function(x, y)`), `pressure`
`{min, max}`, `dips` `{touches per dip, load, wipe}`, `drag` (how far the
tip moves while down: a number or `{length, angle}`), `twist`, `cluster`
(0 even .. 1 in clumps, or `{amount, size}`), `feather` (0 by default;
above 0, touches get lighter where coverage is below 1), `clip`,
`mix_jitter`, `seed`.

**`lose(m, {pile=, where=, ...})`** drags a lightly loaded brush across
the mask's edge from the outside in, where `where` (as `edge=`; 1 by
default) is high: short strokes start outside, cross the edge at a slant
(or at `angle`) and lift off inside. Also `tool` (`"filbert 4"`), `reach`
(`{out, in}` units), `load` (0.2), `pressure` (`{0.35, 0.02}`), `every`
(a stroke every 1.2 brush widths), `seed`. It returns the number of

`work`, `blend` and `stipple` also take `visible=`, `behind=`,

content.text:
# Studio notes

Facts about the canvas, the paint and the tools at this easel, by operation:
what you do, what the paint does and, where it's known, why. Widths and
positions are in canvas units (the canvas is 1000 units wide).

## The canvas and ground

1. The linen's vertical threads are closer-spaced and more even than the
   horizontal ones, which carry thick slubs a few millimeters long.
2. The ground chosen in `canvas{}` shows through thin paint; body color
   hides it.
3. Light paint laid at light pressure over a wet dark catches only the high
   points of the knife-textured ground. The dark stays in the hollows as a
   net of fine dark lines that looks like cracking.
4. Bristles plough paint off the tops of the weave, so a lay-in can keep
   small specks of bare ground. A denser pass covers them.

## Paint in thin films

5. A coat of paint over paint of its own masstone looks the same at any
   thickness, so a mark from a pile matching what it lies on disappears
   into it.
6. A thin film doesn't look like its pile. Thin dark or earth mixtures over
   a pale passage come out lighter, warmer and more saturated than the
   masstone on the palette.
7. The thin fringe of a dark stroke over a light field dries as a warm
   brown halo.
8. Lead white hides strongly (about 0.82 of a full hide per coat); smalt and
   pale smalt are semi-transparent (about 0.3). A thin veil of a pale
   lead-white mixture veils and lightens what is under it, like a scumble,
   rather than tinting it.

## Brushes

9. Every brush is blunt unless given a `point`. A blunt brush's mark runs
   from about half its width at the lightest touch to its full width pressed
   (a little more with splay), so it can't taper to a point.
10. A pointed brush at light pressure lays a hairline, and its width grows
    with pressure. A band a few units wide needs real pressure or a blunt
    brush of that width. A stroke whose pressure falls off at the end draws
    down to the tip and still reaches the end of its path.
11. A brush keeps its paint across strokes. Each stroke lays most at its
    start, and the load runs down along the stroke, so a long drag with a
    wide brush runs dry partway and leaves starved streaks and bands.
12. A well-loaded hair wets the hollows of the weave. A nearly empty one
    skims the tops (dry brush, broken color). Soft hair bends down into the
    hollows; stiff bristle rides on the tops.
13. Dry brush breaks up only at very low loads (well under 0.1 of a full
    load). At loads that still seem light it lays continuous lines or flat
    patches with clean edges. (reported, not verified)
14. A pointed brush loaded below about a quarter stops wetting the hollows,
    and its thin line breaks up along the weave. Run dry, the tip loses its
    point and splits.
15. A pressed touch lays one continuous, nearly round patch (the paint
    bridges the hairs) that grows with pressure.

## Strokes, passes and clipping

16. `clip=true` stops every bristle on the mask's edge, weighted by the
    mask's value. A clipped fill reproduces the mask's outline exactly, as
    one even line, steps and corners included. The `detail` and `blend`
    hands are clipped by default. `broad`, `body`, `hatch`, `glaze` and
    `scumble` are not.
17. Unclipped strokes run past the mask's edge by their own length and
    width. Along a long straight edge they throw lumps into the field
    beyond, and a brush wider than a band spreads well outside it.
18. The square ends of unclipped strokes notch a shape's edge into steps.
19. In `work`, the mask's value only decides where strokes start (at or
    above `threshold`: 0.3, or 0.1 for `detail`). Unclipped, a soft mask
    edge doesn't make a soft paint edge; strokes end where their lengths
    end.
20. `work` leaves the ground showing between its strokes. With `fill=true`
    it looks at its passage afterward and dabs paint into the bare spots its
    strokes left. Single `stroke` and `touch` calls don't fill in.
21. Short strokes planned along a band about one unit wide come out as a
    dashed line: the planner lays them separately, with gaps.
22. Parallel strokes that all break at the same places leave a row of stroke
    ends across the passage, and the outer strokes' ends make a lobed edge.
23. `cut_in` with a round along a curved edge lays short strokes that follow
    it as a string of small bumps.
24. In a smooth lean passage, the loaded starts of broad strokes stay as
    lighter blotches. Blending reduces them but doesn't remove them.

## Wet into wet

25. A brush over open paint lifts some of it and mixes it with its own. A
    clean brush lifts wet paint, less as it sets, and nothing from set or
    dry paint.
26. Light touches into a wet dark dissolve into it. The same touches on
    paint that has set stay where they land.
27. A pale stroke dragged through a wet dark picks up the dark and comes out
    streaked, dirtier and less opaque, so what is underneath shows.
28. A dark stroke laid into a wet pale passage lifts the pale and comes out
    paler than its pile.
29. A passage laid against a wet neighbor drags the neighbor into its edge.
30. Crossing strokes in wet paint thin each other at the crossings, and the
    layer below shows there.
31. A tacky surface grabs: a brush dragged over it leaves its paint sooner
    and in broken patches (stick and slip).

## Stippling

32. Touches into a wet layer lift some of it and fuse. On a dry layer each
    touch stays separate.
33. One dip serves one small patch of touches (24 by default), and each
    dip's mixture varies a little. On a dry layer the passage can dry as a
    patchwork of slightly different patches; fewer touches per dip make the
    patches smaller.
34. Coverage is how many touches fall on each point; one touch covers about
    π(0.4 × width)².
35. Contrast with what is underneath decides how a stipple reads. A coverage
    that gives a veil over a mid tone gives solid patches over a pale field.
36. With `feather` above 0, touches press lighter where coverage falls
    below 1, so a thinning stipple ends in smaller, fainter marks; at 0 they
    keep their pressure.
37. A row of separate touches along a thin line reads as a string of beads.
    A short dragged stroke along it reads as one continuous ridge.

## Blending

38. The blender fuses open paint by lifting it and moving it. It can't move
    set or dry paint.
39. `blend` stays inside its mask by default. Unclipped, it drags wet paint
    across the mask's edge.
40. Touches stippled into a wet layer and then blended fuse into it. Only
    the strongest contrasts survive, as thin traces. Touches laid after the
    blending pass stay on top as a lacy texture.
41. Repeated blending of one lean layer lifts paint off the tops of the
    weave, and the ground shows through as a pale lattice.
42. Blending spreads each thin spot in a layer into a soft blotch.

## Glazing

43. A brushed glaze (`hand="glaze"`) isn't clipped.
    Over a dry pale passage it lays its thin film mostly on the tops of the
    weave, speckles and, once blended, reads lighter. (reported, not
    verified)

## Masks

44. Every mask covers the whole canvas. A mask function that isn't zero far
    from the spot you mean paints there too.
45. Masks from shapes (`poly`, `rect`, `ellipse`, `ribbon`) are crisp.
    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

# Caspar David Friedrich: materials and method

*A sourced technical report. Every claim cites a source key; the sources
are listed at the end. "Uncertain" marks claims that are unverified,
disputed or taken from a single object.*

## Summary

Friedrich painted in oil on fine, plain-weave linen that he bought already
primed. The grounds had two to four thin layers: a warm lower layer (red
or ocher) under a light, lead-white-rich top layer [KÖR p.284; CATS
p.127]. Over a precise graphite or ink underdrawing he laid a very thin
underpainting, then one or two very thin paint layers [SMB-proj; CATS
p.127]. He used few pigments. Before about 1820 his main blue was smalt, a
semi-transparent cobalt glass; after that, cobalt blue, with chrome yellow
among the yellows [ALF pp.341, 348–349]. Gradations come from stippling
and from thin paint pooling in the fine texture of the ground, not from
thick blending [CATS p.127; NG p.56]. No accessible source gives thread
counts or paint-film thicknesses in microns for his paintings.

**Terms.** *Ground/priming*: the preparatory layers between canvas and
paint. *Cross-section*: a microscopic sample cut through all layers.
*IRR (infrared reflectography)*: imaging that shows carbon-based drawing
under paint. *XRF (X-ray fluorescence)*: elemental analysis. *Glaze*: a
transparent paint layer. *Impasto*: thick, raised paint. *Craquelure*:
the network of cracks in paint or varnish.

## 1. Supports

- **Fabric.** Fine linen canvas; two large canvases of 1808–10 were cut
  from adjoining sections of one roll, established by weave matching
  [CATS p.127 and n.2]. The Dresden paintings use locally grown flax,
  handwoven in plain weave. In his late work he preferred "finer, more
  densely woven canvases" [KÖR p.283].
- **One piece of cloth.** A single strip of canvas whatever the size, so
  even large formats have no seams [KÖR p.283].
- **Thread count.** No count for any of his canvases appeared in
  accessible sources. **Proxy:** canvases bought ready-primed in Dresden in
  1827–34 by another painter measure 10–16 threads/cm in both directions
  [CATS-E pp.45–47].
- **Sizes.** From about 32.5 × 45 cm [RSC p.42] to 110.6 × 171.4 cm [CATS
  p.126].
- **Stretching.** Mostly softwood stretchers with blind mortise-and-tenon
  corners and hardwood wedges [KÖR p.283]. Uneven pull marks (cusping) on
  one edge only of a small canvas suggest it was cut from a larger,
  already-primed length [NG pp.51, 55].
- **Panels.** None documented for his oils in the sources consulted.
  *Uncertain.*

## 2. Grounds

- **Commercial, multi-layer, warm underneath.** Commercially primed canvas
  cut from long lengths; Dresden suppliers sold primed cloth in several
  colors [KÖR p.284]. Two to four thin layers [KÖR p.284]. Lower layers
  hold inexpensive ocher, burnt red earth, chalk and barium sulfate and
  "only served to smooth and even out the weave texture." Upper layers are
  mostly lead white, probably in oil; he painted mostly on "a patchy
  whitish ground" [KÖR p.284].
- **One pair of canvases (1808–10).** Three priming layers: bright red,
  then two light brown. The first two were applied with a spatula; the
  third looks roller-applied and has "a finely textured structure" [CATS
  p.127; SMB-blog]. In a cross-section the red layer holds aluminosilicate
  and iron oxides, followed by several yellow-gray lead-white layers with
  iron oxides, vermilion grains and calcium-rich grains [NPJ25].
- **A small canvas of about 1811.** Two layers, both chalk and lead white
  with a little umber and ocher; the upper has more lead white, so it is
  lighter and cooler. The binder is walnut oil [NG p.55].
- **Tool marks.** X-rays show wavy strokes from priming knives in the lower
  layers. The top layer was brushed, and its bristle striations "shine
  through the thin upper paint layers" [KÖR p.284].
- **Colored grounds.** Some paintings have a reddish-ocher or pink top
  ground that stays visible under loose paint or is left bare in places
  [KÖR p.284; HH].
- **Weave.** The lower layers level the weave [KÖR p.284]; the visible
  micro-texture comes mainly from the top ground (brush striations or
  roller texture).
- **Thickness.** No micron values found. *Gap.*

## 3. Underdrawing

- **Media.** Graphite pencils of different hardness and black chalk,
  sometimes in two passes: a faint first outline, then a bolder one.
  Straight lines were probably ruled [CATS pp.128, 131]. Chalk and pencil
  first, then "quill-pen and ink," is also reported [CATS p.132; NG p.49];
  faint ruled lines (possibly pencil) under thicker ink lines [NG pp.49,
  58].
- **Over his career.** Early works are drawn almost entirely in graphite,
  and the drawing often stays visible through the very thin paint. From
  1811 to the mid- or late 1820s a pen is added and the paint gets denser.
  Late works use a pointed brush, and the drawing is almost fully covered
  [ART, summarizing Mösl 2021].
- **Precision.** "Rich in detail," with "no gradation of detail according
  to significance" [CATS p.132]. Drawn elements were sometimes left
  unpainted [CATS p.128].
- **Through the paint.** Lines "still partly shimmer through" [CATS
  p.132]; traces of drawing show as dark dots at color boundaries [HH].
- **Tools.** A picture of his studio of 1811 shows two palettes, a set
  square, a T-square, a ruler and a maulstick [KÖR/Busch pp.326–327].

## 4. Pigments

| Pigment | Evidence | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Lead white | [CATS p.127]; [NG pp.51, 56] | The main white; in the grounds too |
| Smalt (cobalt potash glass) | [CATS p.127]; [NG p.56]; [ALF] | Several grades from pale gray to deep blue, alone or with lead white [NG p.56]. About 3 wt% Co [NPJ25]. Chosen "on account of its semi-transparent property" [CATS p.127] |
| Ochers and earths (goethite, hematite) | [ALF p.348]; [CATS p.127] | Yellow and red earths |
| Vermilion/cinnabar | [NPJ25]; [KÖR fig. 6] | Small admixtures |
| Red iron oxide | [NG p.56] | A few particles |
| Bone black | [NG p.56] | In a mixture with smalt, Naples yellow, ochre and possibly Prussian blue |
| Naples yellow | [NG p.56] | *Disputed:* XRF found no antimony in the areas it tested [ALF p.349] |
| Prussian blue | "Possibly" [NG p.56]; inferred from K and Fe [ALF Table 2] | |
| Cobalt blue | From 1818/24 [ALF]; "almost entirely replaced smalt… after about 1820" [NG p.56] | |
| Chrome yellow (lead chromate) | 1817 and 1818/24 [ALF] | |
| Green pigments | "a few… green" pigments [CATS p.127]; copper greens and green earth [MÄD p.102] | See §8 |
| Copper blues | No copper detected in the blue areas tested, which excludes azurite there [ALF p.348] | Natural or synthetic ultramarine was *not reported* |

## 5. Binding media

- **Walnut oil** in ground and paint of one small canvas [NG p.55], the
  only published medium analysis found. Linseed or poppy oil, resins and
  driers are *unverified*.
- **Egg white** as a temporary coating over fresh paintings [CATS p.127; KÖR p.283].

## 6. Layers and application

- **Number of layers.** "One to two very thin layers" of paint [SMB-proj].
  One canvas: primings 1–3, underdrawing, underpainting, one smalt paint
  layer, egg white, then later varnishes [CATS fig. 3]. Another: a first
  dark-blue layer, then light blue, pink and white in places [CATS p.127].
  A third: "a single thin layer using remarkably few pigments" [NG p.56].
  A fourth (1807/08): two ocher ground layers, a patchy white ground, a
  thin violet layer (smalt splinters and cinnabar), then a very thin
  pale-yellow layer [KÖR fig. 6].
- **Film thickness.** "Very, very fine layers" [SPK]; a "gossamer-thin
  film" [CATS p.127]. No micron values found. *Gap.*
- **Pooling.** The thin paint "accumulated in the depths of the textured
  ground layers," producing the finest dots of color and "almost
  continuous gradations" without visible brushstrokes [CATS p.127].
- **Stippling.** Some passages are stippled, which "enhance[s] the
  transparency and light scattering" [NG p.56; KÖR fig. 7].
- **Strokes.** Early brushwork is "painstaking… small strokes of paint
  placed side by side like a closely woven textile" [NG pp.49–50]. Paint
  was modeled while still wet [MOST-abs].
- **Impasto.** Limited in early works [NG p.50]; some later works mix thick
  and thin paint and leave the ground bare in places [HH].
- **Order of work.** Ground (bought), then underdrawing, then a "very thin
  underpainting," then paint [CATS p.127]; small details were added last,
  over finished passages [NG p.56; CATS p.130]. Brush types (sable or
  bristle) are *undocumented* in these sources.

## 7. Condition and aging

- **Fragility.** The thin paint made the paintings "exceptionally prone to
  damage" [SMB-proj]; many micro-losses come from abrasion in past
  cleaning [SMB-blog].
- **Smalt discoloration.** Smalt has partly lost its color in one painting:
  low potassium (4.9 wt%) and changed cobalt coordination show an
  intermediate stage of degradation; a simulation of the original colors
  comes out cooler and bluer [NPJ25; SMB-blog]. Smalt can turn brown over
  time [HH].
- **Craquelure.** One painting has an elongated craquelure, probably from
  pressure on the back [HH].
- **Pentimenti.** Few [NG p.49; ART; CATS p.129].

## 8. Greens

- **Mostly mixed.** The Dresden team (14 paintings) writes that "the
  palette was very sparing" but the greens show a "lush variety"
  ("üppige Vielfalt"). The true greens were "copper-containing pigments
  and green earth." Greens were often mixed from blue and yellow: Prussian
  blue "very often," smalt and cobalt blue as well, with yellow ocher,
  Naples yellow or chrome yellow [MÄD p.102]. Green passages often have
  "several (up to four) layers of different greens" [MÄD p.102].
- **One painting of 1808.** XRF found Cu and As in the same layer, with no
  intact copper arsenite: the authors assume a degraded Scheele's or
  Schweinfurt green [MÄD p.102]. *Single object.* Since 1808 predates
  Schweinfurt green (1814), this would be Scheele's green unless the layer
  is later (*inferred*).
- **Rinmann's green**, rare, found on three paintings of about 1819–23
  [MÄD p.102 n.3; MOST-abs].
- **A dating test.** A painting was de-attributed partly because its greens
  are cobalt blue mixed with chrome yellow, anachronistic for its supposed
  date of 1798/99 [MÄD p.102].

| Green | Date and availability | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Green earth (terre verte) | Ancient; in painters' manuals through the 19th century | [AP1 pp.143–144, 147] |
| Verdigris / copper resinate | Old; "rarely found in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century paintings"; around 1816 still made as green "varnishes" | [AP2 pp.132, 149] |
| Scheele's green (copper arsenite) | "Introduced in 1778"; "use as an artist's pigment is little documented" | [AP3 p.221] |
| Schweinfurt/emerald green | Made from 1814; a trade secret until 1822; sold in tubes from 1832; earliest easel finds c.1832 | [AP3 pp.222–223, 259; WEB-em] |
| Rinmann's green (cobalt-zinc oxide) | 1780; "poor tinting strength and high cost… kept it in limited use" | [WEB-co] |
| Chromium oxide (opaque) | "Rarely used because of its high price" (1831); earliest finds 1845–50 | [AP3 p.275] |
| Viridian | Made c.1838, patented 1859, earliest finds 1863 | [AP3 pp.274–275; CL-vir] |
| Chrome green (chrome yellow + Prussian blue) | Appeared shortly after chrome yellow; chrome yellow made commercially in Germany only from 1820 | [AP1 p.189; AP3 pp.203–204; MÄD p.102] |

Green earth is translucent, weak and short of body [AP1 p.146; FIELD
p.129].

## Sources

- **[RSC]** Royal Society of Chemistry, *The Chemistry of Art*, case study 9. https://edu.rsc.org/download?ac=14318
- **[SMB-blog]** Mösl and Schneider, "In neuem Glanz," 2016. h

content.thinking:
I've marked this final before, having put in 285 chunks and 353 days, but since I'm invited to keep developing until truly complete, I want to look at it fresh and critically rather than assume the prior verdict holds. Let me examine it again at full view, in 1:1 crops, and through value and squint checks to see if it really holds up.

The sky's gradient reads nicely but feels a touch too smooth and "digital" compared to Friedrich's thin, layered strata — otherwise the composition captures his spirit well, with the gnarled oak, lone figure, and distant ruin. The oak's twig detail is strong, though the flat dark trunk mass may need more modulation, and the water and reflection look convincing if a bit smudgy. The foreground bank feels overly flat and featureless — Friedrich's dark masses usually carry at least subtle texture even when large and simplified.

The composition flows well, guiding the eye from tree to figure to ruin, and elements like the pale mist bank on the right and the spiky reeds work fine, but I want to zoom in and examine crops at full resolution before deciding whether targeted refinements would genuinely help or risk overworking a piece already called final.

content.thinking:
The painting reads well overall—the oak silhouette, sky gradient, calm water, and distant ruin all work, with a solid composition of tree left, open right, and the ruin as focal point. But looking critically, I notice a pale lilac shape on the far right hill that seems off and needs fixing.

The upper sky also has a slight canvas-weave speckle pattern showing through the blue in one area, which might need a thin glaze to smooth over, though it's a minor, manageable fix.

The rest checks out well: the mid-sky has some soft, slightly smeared cloud puffs that read acceptably, the water shows calm reflections with a plausible pale diagonal wedge and fine streaks, and the dark foreground bank could use a touch more warm edge texture where it meets the water.

The bank itself is uniformly dark with only a hint of texture; given the sun sits far right at the horizon and the slope faces that direction, it could plausibly catch a little warm light on its upper surface, similar to Friedrich's subtle brown/green modulations in backlit foregrounds rather than staying a flat, featureless mass.

Adding a thin warm rim along the bank's crest would help separate it from the water, since currently that edge reads as a crisp, uninterrupted dark line. The small cloaked Rückenfigur with a staff by the crest works well, but the trunk's flat black lower section looks too smooth and vector-like — some bark texture is needed so it doesn't read as a cutout against the backlit scene.

I keep going back and forth on the trunk: past attempts at orange ridges failed and a glaze left an odd olive rectangle before I settled on a unified dark coat, and my instinct says a flat dark trunk against the glow is right. But I worry the piece overall feels too clean and digital in places like the trunk and bank — a stronger painting would have subtle painterly variation in those dark masses, like faint warm reflected light on the trunk's lower-left and cool sky light catching the tops of the limbs, and since everything's dry now I can work into those passages without risk of muddying wet paint.

Before touching anything I want to check what's actually dry — I'll query the drying state at several points near where I left off around day 353, and if needed just wait a few weeks since the painting clock costs nothing. Then I'm weighing low-risk improvements: maybe a thin glaze on the sky's upper-right weave pattern if it looks bad up close, or adding subtle modeling to the bank with small tufts or stones now that the paint beneath is safely dry.

That hanging limb cluster near the water reads fine as a drooping branch. Now I want to zoom into 1:1 crops of each region — sky top-right, water, bank, and tree — to check for stray marks or blotches.

content.thinking:
Zooming into the sky at 1:1, I notice a weave-dot pattern and some swirl "fingerprint" marks near the top-right area from paint being lifted during blending—subtle at full view but visible up close, maybe worth softening with a thin cool glaze. Now looking at the ruin area with its dark silhouette.

Not disastrous though. I'm thinking the right hill could use improvement — some darker lilac-blue at its foot where it meets the water, subtle texture at the top edge suggesting fields or trees, and softening that wedge-like left edge so it reads less like a pasted shape. There's also a dark waterline under the shore with a ripple band beneath, and the reflection layer has a patchy, woven, painterly quality worth examining. Next I want to check the far village shore, the tree's base, the bank, the figure, and the reeds at bottom-right before deciding on fixes.

Looking closer at the bank's coloring, I'm noting the olive-brown tone with subtle variation and a thin warm crest line. I'm also spotting a couple of odd geometric shapes at the trunk's base—a small dark horn-like protrusion on the left and a rectangular bit further up the trunk, and I'm pinning down their approximate coordinates in canvas units.

The boxy flat-bottomed foot works partly because the trunk value is close to the bank value, letting it vanish naturally, but it still reads as a pedestal-like shape in the wider view. local function stem(x, y, len, lean, bend, w, headlen, seed)
  math.randomseed(seed)
  local pts = {}
  for i = 0, 7 do
    local t = i / 7
    pts[#pts+1] = {x + lean * len * t + bend * len * t * t + rand(-0.2, 0.2) * t, y - len * t + (i == 0 and 2 or 0)}
  end

  local pr = math.min(1, RG:pressure_for(w) + 0.02)
  RG:stroke(pts, {pressure={pr, 0.25}, ramps={0, 0}})
  local e, p = pts[#pts], pts[#pts - 2]
  local dx, dy = e[1] - p[1], e[2] - p[2]
  local L = math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy); dx, dy = dx / L, dy / L

end

local function stamp_path(pts, r0, r1)
  for i = 1, #pts - 1 do
    local p, q = pts[i], pts[i+1]
    local d = math.sqrt((q[1]-p[1])^2 + (q[2]-p[2])^2)
    local n = math.max(1, math.ceil(d / 0.7))
    for j = 0, n do
      local t = j / n
      local f = ((i - 1) + t) / (#pts - 1)
      stamp(p[1] + (q[1]-p[1]) * t, p[2] + (q[2]-p[2]) * t, r0 + (r1 - r0) * f)
    end
  end
end

function stratum(x0, x1, yc, th, tilt, seed, amp, bodyp, litp)
  local nz = noise{seed=seed, octaves=3, period=55, persistence=0.55}
  local nz2 = noise{seed=seed + 9, octaves=2, period=12, persistence=0.5}
  local function yline(x, t) return yc + tilt * (t - 0.5) + 2.5 * nz(x, 7) end
  local function tapf(t) return math.sin(math.pi * clamp(t, 0, 1)) ^ 0.55 end
  local body = function(x, y)
    if x < x0 or x > x1 then return 0 end
    local t = (x - x0) / (x1 - x0)
    local ty = th * (0.5 + 0.7 * tapf(t)) * (0.8 + 0.4 * nz(x, 44))
    local d = (y - (yline(x, t) - 0.18 * ty)) / (0.5 * ty)
    return amp * math.exp(-d * d * 1.7) * tapf(t) * (0.7 + 0.5 * (nz2(x, y) * 0.5 + 0.5))
  end
  local lit = function(x, y)
    if x < x0 or x > x1 then return 0 end
    local t = (x - x0) / (x1 - x0)
    local ty = th * (0.5 + 0.7 * tapf(t)) * (0.8 + 0.4 * nz(x, 44))
    local d = (y - (yline(x, t) + 0.42 * ty)) / (0.3 * ty)
    return 0.85 * amp * math.exp(-d * d * 1.7) * tapf(t) * (0.6 + 0.6 * (nz2(x + 40, y) * 0.5 + 0.5))
  end
  local band = rect(x0 - 10, yc - th * 1.6 - 6, x1 - x0 + 20, th * 3.2 + 12) * SKYCLOUD
  stipple(band, {pile=bodyp, width=3.0, coverage=body, pressure={0.22, 0.45}, drag={14, 0}, cluster=0.3, seed=seed, dips={16, 0.7, 0.5}, clip=SKYCLOUD})
  stipple(band, {pile=litp,  width=2.6, coverage=lit,  pressure={0.2, 0.42},  drag={12, 0}, cluster=0.3, seed=seed + 1, dips={16, 0.7, 0.5}, clip=SKYCLOUD})
  return band
end

    local ca, sa = math.cos(tilt), math.sin(tilt)

function polyline_at(pts, t)
  -- position and direction at fraction t of a polyline's length
  local L, segs = 0, {}
  for i = 1, #pts - 1 do
    local d = math.sqrt((pts[i+1][1]-pts[i][1])^2 + (pts[i+1][2]-pts[i][2])^2)
    segs[i] = d; L = L + d
  end
  local target = t * L
  local acc = 0
  for i = 1, #pts - 1 do
    if acc + segs[i] >= target or i == #pts - 1 then
      local u = (segs[i] > 0) and (target - acc) / segs[i] or 0
      u = clamp(u, 0, 1)
      local x = pts[i][1] + (pts[i+1][1] - pts[i][1]) * u
      local y = pts[i][2] + (pts[i+1][2] - pts[i][2]) * u
      return x, y, math.atan(pts[i+1][2] - pts[i][2], pts[i+1][1] - pts[i][1])
    end
    acc = acc + segs[i]
  end
end

    cx = cx + math.cos(a) * st

  for _, p in ipairs(top) do pts[#pts+1] = p end

function poplar(x, h, w, seed)

content.text:
**Title: *Lagoon at Dusk, with an Old Oak***

This is a stag-headed oak on a dark bank, seen against the last light over a windless lagoon. The oak's twigs and hairs taper to points. Behind it the sky grades from a deep smalt blue at the top, through lemon, to apricot at the horizon. Thin violet cloud strata with gold undersides converge on the place where the sun has just gone, and a seven-bird flock and an evening star sit in the warm sky. The water carries the glow and, near the viewer, the deeper blue of the upper sky. A ruined gable and four firs stand on a far knoll with their reflections below. A low far shore with a village spire runs behind them. A small figure with a staff stands at the crest beside the oak, and a broken row of fishing stakes leads the eye out across the water to the ruin.

This session I went through the whole picture again and found one real flaw, at the oak's foot, where two pointed roots stuck out and the base ended in a hard, flat edge. It took several repairs to fix, and the early ones made it worse before the later ones helped. It now reads as a plain trunk sinking into the dark ground, and I cleared two side effects of the repairs:
- A dark wedge my mask had left on the water.
- The grass blades that the water patch had covered.

Some faults remain and I've accepted them:
- A faint weave-dot texture in the upper sky, where blends lifted paint.
- A slightly paler patch in the water above the crest.
- A very thin lighter line along the trunk's bottom edge at 1:1.
